package_info.package_manager: Windows DLL (PE file, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (multiple trojanized builds, see IOCs for hashes)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is a trojanized version of the legitimate sqlite3.dll, modified to include malicious code for persistence, data exfiltration, anti-forensics, and as a loader for additional payloads. It is used in a sophisticated APT campaign (Operation CuckooBees) attributed to APT41, enabling stealthy code execution, system reconnaissance, and evidence removal.

execution_context.trigger: At DLL load-time (when sqlite3.dll is loaded by a process, e.g., via rundll32.exe or a parent application)
execution_context.file_location: sqlite3.dll (maliciously modified PE DLL, typically dropped in system or application directories)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At DLL load-time, the code decrypts an embedded or downloaded payload using AES or ChaCha20, loads the decrypted code into memory, and executes it, resulting in in-memory deployment of additional malicious functionality.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate sqlite3.dll should not contain cryptographic routines to decrypt and execute additional payloads at load-time, nor should it perform in-memory code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A standard DLL, especially a database library like sqlite3.dll, is expected to provide only its documented database API and not act as a loader for encrypted or external code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom plugin frameworks may decrypt plugins for extensibility, but this is never expected in a system DLL or a database library context.
key_indicators: Presence of cryptographic routines (AES, ChaCha20) in a database DLL
In-memory decryption and execution of code at DLL load-time
Non-standard code paths in DllMain or exported functions
Absence of legitimate sqlite3.dll functionality or presence of additional export functions

execution_context.trigger: After payload execution (post-infection cleanup phase, typically immediately after malicious actions are completed)
execution_context.file_location: sqlite3.dll (maliciously modified PE DLL, same location as loaded DLL)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the payload has executed, the code overwrites the contents of the malicious sqlite3.dll file with random data and then deletes the file from disk, erasing forensic evidence and hindering post-incident analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate DLLs do not self-delete or overwrite their own contents with random data after being loaded and used.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal DLLs remain static and persistent on disk for reuse and integrity; self-deletion and anti-forensics are not expected behaviors.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Self-deleting installers or updaters may remove themselves after installation, but DLLs loaded by other processes should not erase themselves.
key_indicators: File overwrite with random or pseudo-random data
Immediate file deletion of the DLL after execution
Absence of the DLL on disk after process termination
Anti-forensic routines embedded in a DLL

execution_context.trigger: When a specific export function is called at runtime (e.g., via rundll32.exe with a third parameter specifying the export)
execution_context.file_location: sqlite3.dll (malicious export function, typically in the same directory as the parent process or in a hijacked system path)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a specific export function is invoked at runtime, the code collects detailed system information (such as OS version, user details, environment variables, and possibly file listings) and transmits this data to a remote command-and-control server, enabling attacker reconnaissance and further targeting.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exported functions in sqlite3.dll should not perform system reconnaissance or exfiltrate data to external servers; such behavior is indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLL exports in sqlite3.dll are limited to database operations and should not initiate network communications or collect system-level information.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Diagnostic or telemetry tools may collect system info, but not within a database DLL or via non-standard export functions.
key_indicators: Exported function with undocumented or non-standard behavior
Network communication to external C2 infrastructure from a DLL
Collection and exfiltration of system or user information
Use of rundll32.exe to invoke non-standard exports

attack_chain.action: Initial infection: The malicious sqlite3.dll is dropped onto the target system, replacing or supplementing the legitimate DLL in application or system directories.
attack_chain.leads_to: The trojanized DLL is present on disk and available to be loaded by legitimate or attacker-controlled processes.

attack_chain.action: DLL load: The trojanized sqlite3.dll is loaded into memory by a process (e.g., via rundll32.exe or a hijacked application), triggering execution of the malicious loader code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Decryption and in-memory execution of the embedded or downloaded payload.

attack_chain.action: Payload execution: The decrypted payload runs in memory, enabling further malicious actions such as system reconnaissance and C2 communication.
attack_chain.leads_to: Collection of system information and exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

attack_chain.action: Anti-forensics: The malicious DLL overwrites its own contents with random data and deletes itself from disk to evade detection and hinder forensic analysis.
attack_chain.leads_to: Removal of forensic evidence, persistence only in memory, and increased difficulty for defenders to recover the original malicious DLL.

behavioral_signatures: DLLs named sqlite3.dll performing cryptographic decryption and in-memory code execution at load-time
DLLs overwriting their own file contents with random data and deleting themselves after execution
Presence of non-standard or undocumented export functions in sqlite3.dll
DLLs loaded via rundll32.exe with unusual or undocumented parameters
sqlite3.dll initiating outbound network connections or C2 communications
file_indicators: sqlite3.dll with unexpected hash values (see provided SHA256 IOCs from threat intelligence)
sqlite3.dll present in unusual directories (e.g., application folders where it is not expected, or replacing legitimate system files)
sqlite3.dll files that are deleted or missing shortly after process execution
sqlite3.dll with additional or modified export functions compared to the official version
network_indicators: Outbound connections from processes loading sqlite3.dll to known C2 domains or IP addresses (as identified in threat intelligence feeds)
Unexpected network activity (e.g., HTTP/S POST, beaconing) originating from processes that have loaded sqlite3.dll
Data exfiltration attempts to external infrastructure following DLL load
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for DLL files named sqlite3.dll with hashes matching known IOCs or with modified export tables. Alert on DLLs that perform cryptographic operations or spawn network connections at load-time. Detect DLLs that overwrite and delete themselves after execution. Monitor for rundll32.exe or other processes loading sqlite3.dll with non-standard export functions or parameters. Correlate file system events with network traffic to known C2 domains or IPs, and flag rapid deletion of DLLs after process execution.
